newsitem.title: HUNGARY: NATO official says new members may buy Russian.
newsitem.headline: NATO official says new members may buy Russian.

text.p: A NATO official said on Wednesday that new members from Central Europe would not be prevented from buying new Russian equipment and would not face minimum requirements for modernising their forces.
"NATO does not do any centralised control of armaments planning, budgeting or procurement," NATO Deputy Secretary General Norman W. Ray told reporters.
"NATO is first and foremost interested in inter-operability. That is the general formula that is applied by NATO to national equipment and capabilities regardless of their source."
Ray earlier met Hungary's Defence Minister Gyorgy Keleti during a visit to Budapest to explain NATO's procurement policy to Hungarian military officials and suppliers.

The front runners for early NATO membership, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland, all have armies which use almost exclusively Soviet-made equipment, much of it obsolete or in need of replacement, and have expressed concern about the cost of upgrading their military to NATO standards.
Russia has offered equipment, especially missiles and fighters, which in many cases would considerably undercut prices offered by Western suppliers.

Ray said new members would be free to order military equipment from Russia and any other supplier provided this did not conflict with military necessity. He also stressed that there was no minimum requirement for new states modernising their forces.

"The allies consider the capability of a nation in order to ensure that collectively we have the best prospect of meeting the requirements of our military forces but there is no minimum requirement," he said.
Prague, Warsaw and Budapest are now preparing multi-million dollar tenders to replace their fleets of ageing Soviet-made MiG fighters.

Western planemakers such as Lockheed, McDonnell Douglas, Saab and Dassault are lining up to bid and Russia's state arms agency Rosvooruzhenie is also reported to be considering offering Su-27s, Su-30s and Su-39s.
Ray denied that a formal decision on inviting the three central European states to join the alliance at a forthcoming NATO summit in Madrid had already been made.

Spanish government sources have said the United States and Spain have agreed that Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic should be invited to join NATO at the summit and Slovenia and Romania should also be considered for membership.
"To the best of my knowledge the NATO nations have not ectively agreed on which nations will offered accession opportunity at Madrid," Ray said.
